\begin{document}

\title{What Can Three Seeds and Fifty Rollouts Resolve?\\ A Preregistered Audit of Operator and Seed Variance on robomimic Multi-Human Benchmarks}

\author{Jaiveer Bassi%
\thanks{J. Bassi is an independent researcher (e-mail: jaiveerbassi@yahoo.com).}%
\thanks{Code, preregistration, partitions, initial states, per-run and per-rollout results: \protect\url{https://github.com/imjbassi/operator-variance-audit}, archived at \protect\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23109850}.}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Results on the robomimic Multi-Human (MH) imitation-learning benchmarks are conventionally reported as a mean over three training seeds, each evaluated with 50 rollouts. We preregistered the hypothesis that the variance caused by \emph{which operators' demonstrations are in the training set} exceeds the variance caused by training seed, and tested it with 138 BC-RNN runs on Lift, Can and Square: ten seeds at fixed data, six leave-one-operator-out partitions, and six size-matched random partitions as a control, all evaluated at the final checkpoint on fixed initial states. The preregistered tests were not met on any task; with six operators the procedure detects a true ratio of two only \OneSqPowTwo\% of the time. What the data do establish concerns the reporting convention. With 50 rollouts on shared initial states, checkpoints trained with different seeds cannot be told apart by success rate on any task; they differ mainly in which states they solve. On Square, two three-seed means must differ by \OneSqMDD{} points to be distinguished. Re-evaluating the same 46 Square checkpoints with 500 rollouts, the seed effect becomes detectable, the 50-rollout success rates correlate only $r=\AgreeR$ with the 500-rollout ones, and an apparent proficiency-tier pattern disappears. At 500 rollouts the operator-partition standard deviation is \TwoSqBSDp{} against \TwoSqCSDp{} for random partitions; that contrast nominally meets the preregistered threshold but does not survive Monte Carlo error, and we do not treat it as established. We give reporting recommendations.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Imitation learning, benchmarking, reproducibility, variance components, learning from demonstration.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{T}{he} robomimic study~\cite{mandlekar2021robomimic} established the most widely used protocol for evaluating offline imitation learning in manipulation: train on a fixed demonstration dataset, evaluate with 50 rollouts, and report success rate averaged over three seeds. Its Multi-Human (MH) datasets, 300 demonstrations per task from six operators of varied proficiency collected with RoboTurk~\cite{mandlekar2018roboturk}, are a standard testbed, and later work reports on them with the same three seeds and 50 evaluation episodes, for example Diffusion Policy and its baselines~\cite{chi2023diffusion}. The three-seed standard deviation is the only uncertainty attached to such numbers.

That standard deviation measures how much the result moves when the optimizer's random stream changes and everything else is fixed. It says nothing about how much the result would move had the dataset contained demonstrations from different people. For a benchmark built from six operators, that second source is not obviously smaller. If it is larger, the conventional uncertainty understates the real one.

We preregistered a test of that claim before any training run. The claim was not supported, and we report that plainly, together with what the experiment did establish, which concerns the measurement rather than the operators:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A preregistered negative result with its power} (Section~\ref{sec:primary}). With six operators the procedure has \OneSqPowTwo\% power at a true ratio of two, so the negative result bounds little.
\item \textbf{At 50 rollouts the seed effect is invisible} (Section~\ref{sec:floor}). An exact paired test finds no difference between ten seeds on any task; checkpoints differ in which states they solve, and that only averages out over many states.
\item \textbf{Fifty rollouts do not characterise a checkpoint} (Section~\ref{sec:stage2}). At 500 rollouts the seed effect on Square is detectable, the 50-rollout numbers explain \AgreeRsq\% of the variance of the 500-rollout ones, and a tier pattern seen at 50 rollouts vanishes.
\item \textbf{Resolvability thresholds and recommendations} (Sections~\ref{sec:resolve} and~\ref{sec:recs}).
\end{itemize}
We cite robomimic as the origin of a convention the field, including this author, has used; nothing here criticises that study, which also released the per-operator labels that make this audit possible.

\section{Related Work}
\textbf{Seeds and statistical practice.} Seed sensitivity and the unreliability of small seed counts are well documented in deep reinforcement learning~\cite{henderson2018matters,colas2018seeds,agarwal2021precipice}. Bouthillier \emph{et al.}~\cite{bouthillier2021variance} showed for supervised benchmarks that data sampling, initialisation and hyperparameters all markedly affect comparisons; our Arm~C is the imitation-learning analogue of their data-resampling source. Kress-Gazit \emph{et al.}~\cite{kressgazit2024empirical} recommend reporting evaluation conditions and statistical uncertainty in robot learning. We measure how the conventional statistic decomposes on a heavily used benchmark.

\textbf{Demonstrator heterogeneity.} The robomimic study analysed MH data by proficiency tier, pooling two operators per tier, to ask how algorithms cope with suboptimal data~\cite{mandlekar2021robomimic}; individual operators were not a unit of analysis. Data quality and the compatibility of demonstrators affect imitation learning~\cite{belkhale2023dataquality,gandhi2022compatible}. Our question is statistical: with the operator as the unit of replication, how much does performance move when one operator is removed, relative to seed and to removing the same number of random demonstrations? We follow preregistration practice~\cite{nosek2018prereg}, with a dated amendment log.

\section{Preregistered Design}
\label{sec:design}
The preregistration, with predictions, falsification criteria and the analysis plan, was committed to the public repository before any training run and is unchanged there, followed by four dated amendments.

\subsection{Data, training and evaluation}
We use the robomimic v1.5 MH low-dimensional datasets for Lift, Can and Square (robosuite~\cite{zhu2020robosuite} 1.5.1): 300 demonstrations each, 50 per operator. Operator identity is read directly from the filter keys shipped in the files (\texttt{better\_operator\_1}, \dots, \texttt{worse\_operator\_2}), which we verified are disjoint, contiguous blocks of 50 covering the dataset. The operator index is defined within a tier and is not documented to denote the same person across tasks, so we make no cross-task statement about individuals.

All runs train BC-RNN with the robomimic low-dimensional hyperparameters (two-layer LSTM of width 400, five-mode Gaussian-mixture head, sequence length 10, Adam at $10^{-4}$, batch 100, 2000 epochs of 100 steps; robomimic v0.5.0). We evaluate only the \emph{final} checkpoint, chosen without reference to evaluation rollouts. The original study reports the maximum over periodic evaluations and itself reports that selecting by validation loss or the last checkpoint instead gives a 10 to 100\% decrease~\cite{mandlekar2021robomimic}, so that figure is optimistic. Our final-checkpoint means on the full datasets are \OneLiftAMean, \OneCanAMean{} and \OneSqAMean; the maximum-over-training figures in~\cite[Table~1]{mandlekar2021robomimic} are 100.0, 100.0 and 78.0, under a different checkpoint rule and dataset version.
% Table 1 values (BC-RNN, low-dim, MH: 100.0 +- 0.0, 100.0 +- 0.0, 78.0 +- 4.3) were read twice from the ar5iv HTML of arXiv:2108.03298 on 2026-10-01.
Each checkpoint is evaluated with 50 rollouts of horizon 500 on 50 initial conditions generated once per task, stored, and reused for every checkpoint. Both the simulator state and the scene model are restored, since robosuite regenerates the model at each reset and Lift randomises the cube size, and the rollout random stream is fixed per rollout index. Re-running a checkpoint reproduced every rollout outcome and step count.

\subsection{Three arms}
\textbf{Arm A (seed):} all 300 demonstrations, ten seeds. \textbf{Arm B (operator composition):} six leave-one-operator-out partitions of 250 demonstrations, three seeds each. \textbf{Arm C (matched random control):} six partitions of 250 demonstrations drawn uniformly at random from the 300, three seeds each. That is 10, 18 and 18 runs per task, 138 runs and 6{,}900 rollouts in total. Arm~C is load-bearing: two Arm~B partitions differ in which operator is absent but also in which demonstrations are present (any two share 200 of 250). Arm~C has the same size and comparable overlap and isolates the second effect. Partition memberships were committed once and never changed.

\subsection{Statistics}
\label{sec:stats}
The unit of replication is the operator (the partition), never the rollout or the demonstration; the per-run statistic is the final-checkpoint success rate $y$.

\emph{Seed spread.} $s_A$ is the standard deviation over the ten Arm~A seeds, with a seed-bootstrap interval, measured on the shared stored states. The binomial floor $\sqrt{\bar p(1-\bar p)/n}$ is the sampling error of one success rate against a fresh draw of $n$ states. On shared states, outcomes are correlated across checkpoints, so the null for ``no difference between seeds'' is the per-state floor $\sqrt{\bar v/n}$, where $\bar v=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i(1-q_i)$ averages over states and $q_i$ is the success rate on state $i$ across checkpoints. The exact test is Cochran's $Q$ on the checkpoints-by-states matrix. Both are post hoc (Amendment~4).

\emph{Variance components.} For Arms~B and~C separately, the $6\times 3$ partition-by-seed table is modelled as $y_{ps} = \mu + a_p + b_s + e_{ps}$ with independent effects of variance $\sigma_p^2$, $\sigma_s^2$, $\sigma_e^2$, estimated by the method of moments, $\hat\sigma_p^2=(\mathrm{MS}_p-\mathrm{MS}_e)/3$ and $\hat\sigma_s^2=(\mathrm{MS}_s-\mathrm{MS}_e)/6$ truncated at zero~\cite{searle1992variance}, and by REML~\cite{patterson1971reml,seabold2010statsmodels}. The residual absorbs rollout noise and partition-by-seed interaction. A zero estimate is a boundary estimate, not evidence of zero variance.

\emph{Contrasts and decision rule.} The headline ratio $R=\sdp^{B}/s_A$ has a percentile interval and one-sided $p$-value from a joint bootstrap~\cite{efron1993bootstrap} over the six partitions and ten Arm~A seeds (2000 resamples). The control contrast $D=(\sdp^{B})^2-(\sdp^{C})^2$, positive when operator partitions vary more than random ones, is bootstrapped over the six partitions of each arm. The primary family, $R>1$ and $D>0$ on three tasks, is corrected by Holm's procedure~\cite{holm1979}; a contrast is supported if its Holm-adjusted one-sided $p$ is below 0.05, with intervals shown unadjusted. The preregistration stated both an interval criterion and Holm correction without saying which governs; Amendment~4 fixes this rule.

\emph{Secondary claim.} Tier labels were predicted not to capture the operator effect, judged by the between-tier share of the Arm~B partition-mean sum of squares against relabelling.

\subsection{Amendments}
\label{sec:amend}
\emph{Amendment 1}, before any data: the tier permutation test has only 15 distinct outcomes ($p\ge 1/15$), so the secondary claim is judged by effect size; power is reported by simulating the headline procedure. \emph{Amendment 2}, after Stage~1 and before any further rollout: \emph{Stage~2} re-evaluates the 46 Square final checkpoints with 500 rollouts on 500 new fixed states, with the same analysis and a two-contrast Holm family; being designed after Stage~1 and reusing its checkpoints, it is a follow-up, not independent confirmation. It also declares three exploratory analyses (Section~\ref{sec:explore}). \emph{Amendment 3} records the Stage~2 outcome and two reporting corrections. \emph{Amendment 4}, after informal review with all results known, fixes the decision rule above and adds the post hoc analyses labelled as such below; \emph{Amendment 5}, after a second informal review, bases paired resolvability thresholds on the larger of $s_A$ and the per-state floor.

\section{Results}
\subsection{The seed effect at 50 rollouts}
\label{sec:floor}
Fig.~\ref{fig:arms} shows every run and Table~\ref{tab:components} the estimates. At fixed data the ten-seed standard deviation is \OneLiftASD{} on Lift, \OneCanASD{} on Can and \OneSqASD{} on Square, where the seeds range over \OneSqARange{} points. \textbf{No task shows a detectable seed effect at 50 rollouts.} Cochran's $Q$ gives $p=\OneLiftCochP$, \OneCanCochP{} and \OneSqCochP{} (Table~\ref{tab:resolve}). Against the binomial floor the picture is the same: the Can spread is below it, and the Lift and Square spreads exceed it by amounts a $\chi^2_9$ test does not distinguish from zero ($p=\OneLiftChiBp$, \OneSqChiBp). The checkpoints are not identical: on Square \OneSqDiscrim{} of the 50 states are solved by some seeds and not others. Seeds differ far more in \emph{which} states they solve than in how many, and that only averages out over many states.

\subsection{Preregistered primary tests (Stage 1)}
\label{sec:primary}
\textbf{The primary claim is not supported on any task.} $R=\OneSqR$ $[\OneSqRlo, \OneSqRhi]$ on Square, \OneLiftR{} on Lift and \OneCanR{} on Can, all with Holm $p=\OneSqRpHolm$. The control contrast is positive on Square (partition SD \OneSqBSDp{} in Arm~B, \OneSqCSDp{} in Arm~C) but not supported ($p=\OneSqDp$, Holm \OneSqDpHolm). On Can the random partitions vary more than the operator partitions; on Lift, at ceiling, several components are at the boundary. The two estimators agree everywhere.

\textbf{This negative result is weak evidence about effect size.} Simulating the preregistered procedure at the fitted noise levels (Fig.~\ref{fig:power}), power on Square is \OneSqPowTwo\%, \OneSqPowThree\% and \OneSqPowFour\% at true ratios of two, three and four, and no better elsewhere. Six partitions give five degrees of freedom, and a bootstrap over six clusters is unreliable~\cite{cameron2008bootstrap}. The denominator $s_A$ also contains the rollout noise floor while the numerator is residual-corrected, so the ratio is conservative by construction. At a true ratio of one the interval excluded one in at most \FPmaxCount{} of 200 simulations per task; that is consistent with a rate below the nominal 2.5\%, but too few runs to show it (exact upper bound \FPupper\%). We noted this when Arm~A finished, recorded it before any Arm~C result existed, and did not alter the test.

\caption{Power of the preregistered headline procedure (probability that the 95\% interval for $R$ excludes one) versus the true ratio, simulated at each task's fitted noise levels. Solid: 50 rollouts; dashed: Square at 500. Each point is 200 simulations (Monte Carlo SE up to 3.5 points).}
\label{fig:power}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Stage 2: the same checkpoints at 500 rollouts}
\label{sec:stage2}
\textbf{A 50-rollout success rate is a poor measurement of a checkpoint} (Fig.~\ref{fig:stages}). Across the 46 checkpoints the two evaluations correlate at $r=\AgreeR$. Their differences have standard deviation \AgreeSD, matching the binomial expectation of \AgreeExp, and reach \AgreeMax{} points. The 50-state set was also \AgreeMean{} points harder on average, so results on a small fixed set are conditional on it.

\textbf{The seed effect becomes visible.} The ten-seed standard deviation is \TwoSqASD{} $[\TwoSqASDlo, \TwoSqASDhi]$, against floors of \TwoSqBinom{} (binomial) and \TwoSqStateFloor{} (per-state). Cochran's $Q=\TwoSqCochQ$ on \TwoSqCochDf{} degrees of freedom ($p=\TwoSqCochP$): seeds produce checkpoints whose success rates differ with a standard deviation of about \TwoSqSDck. Fifty states could not resolve this.

\textbf{The operator contrast nominally meets the preregistered threshold; we do not treat it as established.} The partition standard deviation is \TwoSqBSDp{} in Arm~B and \TwoSqCSDp{} in Arm~C, with equal residuals (\TwoSqBSDe). $R=\TwoSqR$ $[\TwoSqRlo, \TwoSqRhi]$ is not supported ($p=\TwoSqRp$). For $D$, the preregistered bootstrap gives $D\times10^{3}=\TwoSqD$ $[\TwoSqDlo, \TwoSqDhi]$, $p=\TwoSqDp$, Holm \TwoSqDpHolm. \emph{As preregistered, this meets the threshold}, under the rule of Section~\ref{sec:stats} and under an unadjusted interval criterion, but not robustly: the Monte Carlo standard error of the Holm $p$ is \TwoSqDmcSEHolm, well above the margin of 0.001. After seeing this we enumerated the bootstrap exactly (462 distinct resamples of six partitions), which gives $p=\TwoSqDExp$, Holm \TwoSqDExpHolm, interval $[\TwoSqDExLo, \TwoSqDExHi]$. Not claiming the contrast is therefore a conservative choice made after the fact. Both stages put operator partitions above random ones; the data are consistent with an operator effect several times the resampling effect, and equally with none that six operators can establish.

\textbf{More rollouts lower power at a fixed ratio}, from \OneSqPowTwo\% to \TwoSqPowTwo\% at a ratio of two (Fig.~\ref{fig:power}). Because $s_A$ more than halved, a ratio of two now means a partition SD of only \TwoSqPowSdp, \TwoSqPowRatio{} times the Arm~B residual rather than \OneSqPowRatio{} times; the residual, which includes partition-by-seed interaction, shrank less. Simulation error is about \OneSqPowSE{} points per estimate.

\subsection{Tier labels}
\label{sec:tier}
At 50 rollouts the Square partitions looked like a tier effect: holding out either ``better'' operator gave \OneSqDropBOne{} and \OneSqDropBTwo, against at most \OneSqBMeanHi{} for the others, a between-tier share of \OneSqTierShare{} against a null mean of \OneSqTierNull. Even then it was a two-operator pattern: exactly \OneSqPairsReach{} of the 15 ways of pairing the six partitions reach the observed share, precisely those keeping the two ``better'' operators together (permutation $p=\OneSqTierP$), and the tier pairing ranks third among them. At 500 rollouts it is gone: the between-tier share is \TwoSqTierShare, \TwoSqPairsReach{} of 15 pairings reach it, within-tier differences (\TwoSqTierWithin) match between-tier ones (\TwoSqTierBetween), and the first ``better'' partition moved from \OneSqDropBOne{} to \TwoSqDropBOne. Amendment~3 withdrew our Stage~1 statement that the secondary prediction was contradicted; we make no tier claim in either direction. A pattern across six three-seed, 50-rollout means was strong enough to be written down and did not survive ten times the rollouts.

\subsection{What the convention can resolve}
\label{sec:resolve}
Two methods reported as means of $k$ seeds differ detectably at a two-sided 95\% level only if their true difference exceeds roughly
\begin{equation}
\Delta_{\min} \approx 1.96\, s\,\sqrt{2/k}, \qquad s^2 \approx \sigma_{c}^2 + v/n,
\label{eq:mdd}
\end{equation}
where $\sigma_c^2$ is the variance of checkpoints' true success rates across seeds. If both methods use the same stored states (paired), $v=\bar v$; if each draws its own states (unpaired), as with unseeded resets, $v=p(1-p)$, which is never smaller. For the paired case we estimate $s$ by the larger of $s_A$ and the per-state floor, since $s_A$ is a noisy ten-seed estimate: on Can it falls below the floor (\OneCanASD{} against \OneCanStateFloor, interval reaching zero), and using it directly would give an optimistic \OneCanMDDraw{} points. Here the per-state and binomial floors nearly coincide, so pairing gains little. For $k=3$ (Table~\ref{tab:resolve}), Square at 50 rollouts needs \OneSqMDD{} points paired (\OneSqMDDt{} with a $t$ quantile) and \OneSqMDDu{} unpaired, and \TwoSqMDD{} paired at 500 rollouts. These thresholds cover seed and rollout noise only, not demonstration resampling (Arm~C partition SD \TwoSqCSDp{} on Square at 500 rollouts) or any operator effect.

\subsection{Exploratory analyses}
\label{sec:explore}
Declared exploratory in Amendment~2, not tests of the preregistered claims: (i)~with the binomial floor removed from its denominator, $R$ is \OneSqRCorr{} on Square at 50 rollouts and \TwoSqRCorr{} at 500, but the correction is undefined in \OneSqRCorrFloorFrac\% and \TwoSqRCorrFloorFrac\% of resamples; (ii)~the exact $F$-test for a partition component gives $p=\OneSqBFp$ in Arm~B against \OneSqCFp{} in Arm~C on Square at 50 rollouts, and \TwoSqBFp{} against \TwoSqCFp{} at 500, with no test below 0.05 on Lift or Can; (iii)~partitions holding out a ``better'' operator are \OneSqDropDiff{} points below the rest at 50 rollouts and \TwoSqDropDiff{} at 500. These are consistent with a partition effect in Arm~B on Square and change no preregistered decision.

\section{Discussion and Recommendations}
\label{sec:recs}
The hypothesis we registered was about operators; the clearest finding is about rollouts. With 50 rollouts the evaluation cannot see differences between seeds on any of the three tasks, so a three-seed standard deviation describes the measurement more than the method, and on Square the point estimate is a weak proxy for the same checkpoint's success rate under a larger evaluation. The motivating statement, that comparisons a few points apart are not resolvable from the reported statistic, holds on Square for a more elementary reason than the one we proposed. The operator question remains open: both stages order the Square point estimates the same way, neither establishes the effect, and at 500 rollouts power at a ratio of two is still \TwoSqPowTwo\%. A dataset with more operators is required. We recommend:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Report the rollout noise next to the seed SD, and test the seed effect on shared states.} A seed SD near $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ means the evaluation may not see the seed effect; with stored states, Cochran's $Q$ on per-rollout outcomes is an exact test of whether checkpoints differ at all.
\item \textbf{Use enough rollouts for the success band.} Near 60\% success, 50 rollouts give a standard error of 7 points per checkpoint and 500 give 2; Eq.~(\ref{eq:mdd}) states what a budget can resolve.
\item \textbf{Fix and publish the initial conditions and per-rollout outcomes,} including the scene model where it is randomised, on a set large enough that conclusions are not conditional on it.
\item \textbf{Evaluate a checkpoint chosen without the evaluation rollouts}, and \textbf{state the training-set composition} when using subsets of a multi-operator dataset, without reading structure from a handful of low-rollout partition means.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Limitations}
Six operators per task is the binding limitation and sets the power of every operator-level test. The study uses one architecture, low-dimensional observations, one training length, simulation only, one benchmark family, and three seeds per partition. Partitions within an arm overlap heavily, so the random-effects model is an approximation; Arm~C shares that structure, which is why the contrast with it is the meaningful quantity. Stage~2 was designed after Stage~1 and reuses its checkpoints. The exact enumeration was added after the Stage~2 contrast was seen at the boundary, and the preregistered computation alone would have supported that contrast. The per-state floor, Cochran's test, unpaired thresholds and explicit decision rule were added after review and change no Stage~1 decision.

\section{Conclusion}
We preregistered the claim that operator composition contributes more variance than training seed on the robomimic Multi-Human benchmarks, ran 138 training runs with a matched random control, and did not confirm it; the experiment was underpowered for that claim by the number of operators, not by compute. It was well powered for a different conclusion: with 50 rollouts the conventional three-seed statistic cannot detect differences between seeds on any task, cannot resolve differences between methods smaller than about \OneSqMDD{} points on Square, and produced a tier pattern that a tenfold larger evaluation did not reproduce. The preregistration and amendments, partitions, stored initial conditions, per-rollout results for both stages (6{,}900 and 23{,}000 rollouts), and the scripts that regenerate every number, table and figure here are archived at \url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23109850}.
